### Problem: Merge Intervals {#sec-int-p1-a}

::: {.p-statement}
An array `intervals` of $n$ intervals $[a_i, b_i]$ ($1 \le n \le 10^4$, $0 \le a_i \le b_i \le 10^4$). Merge all **overlapping** intervals and return the array of non-overlapping intervals that covers exactly the same set of points. Two intervals count as overlapping if they share at least one point, so $[1,3]$ and $[3,4]$ merge into $[1,4]$.

Source: [LC 56 · Merge Intervals](https://leetcode.com/problems/merge-intervals/){.solved difficulty="Medium"}

Example: `[[1,3],[2,6],[8,10],[15,18]]` → `[[1,6],[8,10],[15,18]]`.
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Overlap is a *pairwise* relation, so the definition of the answer is "$O(n^2)$" — but sorting by start collapses it. Once the intervals are ordered left-to-right, any interval that overlaps the current block must have its start inside the block, so a single running `cur_end` variable decides everything: extend or open new. This is @sec-srt's "sort first" purchase spent on the *merge* relation. The subtle bug that catches almost everyone is comparing an interval to the *previous original* end instead of the *current block* end; nested intervals like $[1,10],[2,3],[4,5]$ then shrink the block incorrectly.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Pairwise passes until stable.** Repeatedly scan for any overlapping pair, merge that pair, and restart. Correct by definition, $O(n^3)$ worst case — the oracle.
2. **Sort by start, then a stack of blocks.** Sort once; walk with a stack whose top is the block currently being grown. Extend the top when the next interval overlaps, push a new block otherwise. $O(n\log n)$, $O(n)$ extra space (the stack).
3. **Sort by start, then a running end.** Same walk, but the "stack" has been collapsed into a `out[-1][1]` cell because the only block you ever modify is the last one. $O(n\log n)$ time, $O(n)$ for the output (in-place variant is $O(1)$ extra).

**Invariant.** `out` is a list of disjoint, maximally-merged blocks over `intervals[:k+1]`, sorted by start. Because the input is sorted, no future interval can start strictly to the left of the current block, so only the *last* block's end ever changes.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Merge any overlapping pair, repeat

::: {.form-next}
Scan for any pair $(i, j)$ whose intervals overlap, replace them with their union, and re-scan. When a full pass produces no merges, you are done. Slow ($O(n^3)$ worst case — up to $n^2$ pair comparisons per pass, $O(n)$ passes, $O(n)$ rebuild per merge) but *it is the definition*.

**Worked example.** $[[1,3],[2,6],[8,10],[15,18]]$: pass 1 sees pair $(0,1)$ overlap on $[2,3]$, merges to $[1,6]$, and the list becomes $[[1,6],[8,10],[15,18]]$. Pass 2 finds no overlapping pair, so we stop — same answer as the fast form.
:::

```{python}

#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("merge", "brute")
    assert str(final) == "[[1, 6], [8, 10], [15, 18]]"
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def merge_brute(intervals):
    cur = sorted([list(x) for x in intervals])
    while True:
        changed = False
        for i in range(len(cur)):
            for j in range(i + 1, len(cur)):
                if cur[i][0] <= cur[j][1] and cur[j][0] <= cur[i][1]:
                    new = [min(cur[i][0], cur[j][0]), max(cur[i][1], cur[j][1])]
                    cur = cur[:i] + cur[i + 1:j] + cur[j + 1:] + [new]
                    cur.sort()
                    changed = True
                    break
            if changed:
                break
        if not changed:
            return cur
```

##### C++

```cpp
// fragment - brute-force oracle for Merge Intervals
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;
vector<vector<int>> mergeBrute(vector<vector<int>> cur) {
    sort(cur.begin(), cur.end());
    while (true) {
        bool changed = false;
        for (int i = 0; i < (int)cur.size() && !changed; ++i)
            for (int j = i + 1; j < (int)cur.size(); ++j)
                if (cur[i][0] <= cur[j][1] && cur[j][0] <= cur[i][1]) {
                    vector<int> nw = {min(cur[i][0], cur[j][0]), max(cur[i][1], cur[j][1])};
                    vector<vector<int>> nxt;
                    for (int k = 0; k < (int)cur.size(); ++k)
                        if (k != i && k != j) nxt.push_back(cur[k]);
                    nxt.push_back(nw);
                    sort(nxt.begin(), nxt.end());
                    cur = nxt; changed = true; break;
                }
        if (!changed) return cur;
    }
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** The predicate `cur[i][0] <= cur[j][1] and cur[j][0] <= cur[i][1]` is the two-sided overlap test — neither interval starts after the other ends. The rebuilt list `cur[:i] + cur[i+1:j] + cur[j+1:] + [new]` removes both and appends the union. The outer `while True` retries until a pass produces no merge; because each merge strictly reduces $|cur|$, at most $n-1$ rounds run. Sorting between passes keeps the search order deterministic and gives the correct final order for free.

#### Sort by start, grow a stack of blocks

::: {.form-next}
Take the sortedness seriously: `sort` the input by start once, then maintain a **stack of merged blocks**. Read each interval: if its start is inside the top block's range, *extend* the top; otherwise push it as a new block. $O(n\log n)$ time and $O(n)$ extra space for the stack. This form is what you code when you may later need to *enumerate* every block explicitly (e.g. union-length queries), and it exposes the invariant `out is monotone` more visibly than the running-end version.

**Worked example.** Same input sorted to $[[1,3],[2,6],[8,10],[15,18]]$: push $[1,3]$; see $[2,6]$ with $2 \le 3$ extend top to $[1,6]$; see $[8,10]$ with $8 > 6$ push; see $[15,18]$ push. Stack $=[[1,6],[8,10],[15,18]]$.
:::


::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-0056-stack
def merge_stack(intervals):
    stack = []
    for a, b in sorted(intervals):
        if stack and a <= stack[-1][1]:
            stack[-1][1] = max(stack[-1][1], b)
        else:
            stack.append([a, b])
    return stack

for _ in range(300):
    n = random.randint(1, 12)
    ivs = [[random.randint(0, 20), random.randint(0, 20)] for _ in range(n)]
    ivs = [[min(x), max(x)] for x in ivs]
    assert merge_stack(ivs) == merge_brute(ivs)
assert merge_stack([[1, 4], [2, 3]]) == [[1, 4]]   # nested stays put
print("merge_stack OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;
vector<vector<int>> mergeStack(vector<vector<int>> in) {
    sort(in.begin(), in.end());
    vector<vector<int>> st;
    for (auto& iv : in) {
        if (!st.empty() && iv[0] <= st.back()[1])
            st.back()[1] = max(st.back()[1], iv[1]);
        else st.push_back(iv);
    }
    return st;
}

int main() { vector<vector<int>> v{{1,3},{2,6},{8,10},{15,18}}; mergeStack(v); }
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** `sorted(intervals)` orders by start (Python breaks ties by end, which is fine). `stack[-1]` is the current block; `a <= stack[-1][1]` is the "overlaps or touches" test. `max(...)` is the *extend, don't replace* rule (@sec-int-merge's most common bug). Else branch pushes a new block. The stress test checks equality with the $O(n^3)$ oracle on 300 random inputs; `[[1,4],[2,3]]` is the nested-interval case that would fail if you wrote `stack[-1][1] = b` (dropping $4$ to $3$).

#### Sort by start, keep only the running end

::: {.form-next}
Same walk, but the "stack" collapses to a single variable — you *only ever touch the last block*, so the list is the state. Output-shape identical, one less indirection. This is the version you write in an interview, and the version that generalises to *in-place* merging if you reuse the input's storage.

**Worked example.** Sorted $[[1,3],[2,6],[8,10],[15,18]]$: open $[1,3]$; see $[2,6]$, extend `out[-1][1] = max(3,6) = 6`; see $[8,10]$, disjoint, open; see $[15,18]$, open. Output $[[1,6],[8,10],[15,18]]$.
:::

```{python}

V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-0056-scan
def merge(intervals):
    out = []
    for a, b in sorted(intervals):
        if out and a <= out[-1][1]:
            out[-1][1] = max(out[-1][1], b)
        else:
            out.append([a, b])
    return out

for _ in range(300):
    n = random.randint(1, 12)
    ivs = [[random.randint(0, 20), random.randint(0, 20)] for _ in range(n)]
    ivs = [[min(x), max(x)] for x in ivs]
    assert merge(ivs) == merge_brute(ivs)
assert merge([[1, 3], [2, 6], [8, 10], [15, 18]]) == [[1, 6], [8, 10], [15, 18]]
assert merge([[1, 4], [4, 5]]) == [[1, 5]]                 # touching merges (closed)
assert merge([[1, 4], [2, 3]]) == [[1, 4]]                 # nested
print("merge OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;
vector<vector<int>> merge(vector<vector<int>>& in) {
    sort(in.begin(), in.end());
    vector<vector<int>> out;
    for (auto& iv : in) {
        if (!out.empty() && iv[0] <= out.back()[1])
            out.back()[1] = max(out.back()[1], iv[1]);
        else out.push_back(iv);
    }
    return out;
}

int main() { vector<vector<int>> v{{1,3},{2,6},{8,10},{15,18}}; merge(v); }
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** Same skeleton as form 2 with the "stack" renamed to `out` and the "extend top" branch renamed to "extend `out[-1]`". Because we only ever mutate the *last* element of `out`, the two are literally the same algorithm — the middle rung just makes the "block list" explicit. In the LC example $[[1,3],[2,6],[8,10],[15,18]]$ the walk produces $[[1,6],[8,10],[15,18]]$ in a single pass: 1 sort, 4 iterations, 1 extension, 3 openings.
:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Pairwise passes** is $O(n^3)$ time (up to $n$ rounds × $O(n^2)$ pair check × $O(n)$ rebuild) and $O(n)$ space. **Sort + stack** is $O(n\log n)$ + $O(n)$ space. **Sort + running end** is $O(n\log n)$ + $O(n)$ output; the in-place variant reuses the input array with $O(1)$ extra. All three agree on the merged-block *set*, so the stress test can (and does) compare them on random inputs. Once you have the fast form, the sort is the whole cost — every further improvement requires a different input model (streaming, dynamic, tree-based).
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- Touching intervals like $[1,3]$ and $[3,4]$ **do** merge under this problem's closed convention. Flip `a <= out[-1][1]` to `a < out[-1][1]` and you get the half-open behaviour where they stay separate — a bug here.
- Nested intervals $[1,10],[2,3],[4,5]$: the `max()` in the extension is what saves you. Without it the block shrinks.
- Duplicate intervals $[1,3],[1,3]$: correct merge keeps one copy. Test this if your walk skips on `a < out[-1][1]` instead of `a <= out[-1][1]`.
- Single-interval input returns it unchanged; empty input returns empty. Both fall out naturally from the walk.
:::
